The upcoming MacBook Ultra will never come cheap, with a brand-new thinner design, OLED display, and touch functionality—without even counting the price hike driven by rising memory costs. The latest reports indicate that manufacturing costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has always preferred to source components from multiple suppliers in order to improve display reliability while securing the best negotiating leverage, and it had originally hoped to do the same with the MacBook Ultra. However, supply chain sources indicate that Apple has decided to use only a single display supplier……

Apple has three display partners across its product lineup: Samsung, LG, and BOE. BOE has so far only supplied displays for the company's lower-end products, while orders for high-end screens are split between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display ever installed on an Apple product. Combining tandem OLED with touch functionality on the large-sized panels required for a laptop is no easy feat, and the latest supply chain report indicates that Apple has decided to source these screens exclusively from Samsung.

The Elec reports that LG was unable to meet Apple's required production volume.

Apple demanded that the partner respond with large-scale mass production using large-sized substrates. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6-generation OLED production line, while LG Display reportedly explored continuing with its existing 6-generation production line. Although 6-generation lines can produce laptop OLEDs, substrate efficiency and capacity are lower than with 8.6-generation lines. Due to insufficient early production yields, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

It appears that the low volumes LG could produce are not worth the logistical complexity of having two suppliers. LG is not expected to manufacture displays for this flagship MacBook before 2029.

This situation clearly puts Samsung in a stronger position in panel price negotiations, likely driving up Apple's manufacturing costs—and Apple is expected to pass these costs on to consumers, just as it has done with rising memory costs.

Considering the MacBook Ultra's price could be jaw-droppingly expensive, how likely are you to consider upgrading? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
